title: Planning Your 2027 Marketing Budget: What the Research Actually Says
seoTitle: 2027 Marketing Budget Planning: What the Research Says
seoDescription: What research from Gartner, Forrester, BrightLocal and Pew means for 2027 budget planning, what transfers to a local business, and a simple five bucket budget split.
excerpt: The latest research on marketing budgets and how customers choose, sorted into what carries over to a local business and what does not, plus a simple way to split a 2027 budget.
imageAlt: Young professional working on a laptop at a wooden desk in a bright modern office
imageIdea: Young operator at a bright desk with a laptop, modern office.
author: The SocialDM Insights Team
bodyHtml:
Budget season is here, and the research is louder than ever. The big surveys are worth reading, but most of them describe very large companies. This guide sorts what the 2026 research actually says, what carries over to a local business and what does not, and offers a simple way to split a 2027 budget around where customers now look before they call, book or visit.

What did the big budget surveys find?

Two studies set the tone for 2027 planning.

  • Gartner's 2026 CMO Spend Survey found marketing budgets at 7.8% of company revenue in 2026, up from 7.7% in 2025. Marketing leaders put 15.3% of their budgets toward AI on average, yet only 30% reported mature AI readiness. Keep the sample in mind: 401 marketing leaders in North America, the UK and Europe, most at companies with more than $1 billion in annual revenue.
  • Forrester's 2027 Budget Planning Guides, released July 15, 2026, report that 91% of marketers expect budget increases in 2027. Among Forrester's recommendations is to increase investment in answer engine optimization, meaning brand visibility in answers from AI tools.

The headline for 2027: budgets are steady to rising, and attention is moving toward AI. The open question for a local business is what that should change on the ground.

What changed for local customers?

The bigger shift is in how people choose a local business.

  • AI tools jumped. In BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey of 1,002 US adults, use of ChatGPT and other AI tools for local recommendations rose from 6% to 45% in one year, making AI the third most popular source of business recommendations.
  • Reviews still decide. The same survey found 97% of consumers read reviews for local businesses, and 47% will not use a business with fewer than 20 reviews.
  • Google's lead is shrinking. Google is still the most used review site, but its share fell from 83% in 2025 to 71% in 2026.
  • Clicks are harder to earn. Pew Research Center found that Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, compared with 15% when none did. That data is from March 2025, so treat it as direction, not today's exact rate.

Put together, customers are reading more about you in more places and clicking through less. A 2027 budget should be built for that.

What does not transfer to a local business?

Two things in the big surveys are easy to misread.

The percent of revenue figure is not a rule. Gartner's 7.8% comes mostly from companies with more than $1 billion in revenue. A practice, salon, brokerage or apartment community may need far less or far more depending on how new its location is, how competitive its market is and how much each new customer is worth. Our advice: start from your own numbers, not someone else's average.

"AI budget" can mean two very different things. For a large company it is often software and staff. For a local business, the AI question that matters most is whether AI tools describe you accurately and include you when customers ask. Those are not the same purchase, and only the second one shows up in your calls and bookings.

A simple way to split a 2027 budget

In our view, a local business budget works best in five buckets, funded roughly in this order. We are not prescribing percentages here, because the right mix depends on your market and goals.

BucketWhat it pays forHow to judge it
FoundationA fast website with accurate hours, services, prices where you can share them, and clear answers to common questionsLeads and calls from the site, fewer "are you open" questions
Google profile and reviewsA complete, current Google Business Profile and a steady, honest flow of new reviews with repliesCalls, direction requests, review count and recency
AI visibilityMaking sure the facts AI tools find about you are consistent across your site, profiles and directoriesHow AI tools describe and list you, checked on a schedule
SocialRegular, real content that shows the people and place behind the businessConsistency, engagement, messages and profile visits
PaidAds that reach people actively searching or likely to need you soonCost per lead or booking, not clicks alone

The order matters. Paid ads send people to your website and profile, and AI tools read your website and profile. If the foundation is weak, every other dollar buys less.

What should you measure in 2027?

If fewer people click, website traffic alone will undercount your marketing. Our advice is to track the actions that lead to revenue: calls, direction requests, bookings, form leads, walk in visits and tours. Add review count and recency, since customers weigh both. Then check how AI tools describe your business and whether the facts are right. A correct answer that never sends a click can still be the reason someone calls.

If you have not yet claimed your business in ChatGPT, see ChatGPT now lets you claim your business for what that program offers and what it does not.

A planning calendar from December

  1. December: Check that your hours, services and contact details match on your website, Google profile and main directories. Write down this month's calls, bookings and review count as your baseline.
  2. January: Fund the foundation and Google profile buckets first. Set a simple, honest review request routine.
  3. February and March: Add social and paid in measured steps, one change at a time so you can see what worked.
  4. April: Compare the first quarter to your December baseline and move money toward what produced calls and bookings.

For industry specific versions, see the 2027 apartment marketing plan and the real estate agent marketing plan for 2027.

Revisit in 2027: we will check these numbers again when Gartner and BrightLocal publish their next editions and update this guide.

Questions we hear

How much should a small business spend on marketing in 2027?

There is no single right percentage. The best known benchmark, Gartner's 7.8% of revenue, comes from a survey of mostly very large companies. In our view, a local business should start from its own numbers: what a new customer is worth and what it costs to win one today.

Should we move budget from SEO to AI search?

In our view, they overlap more than they compete. AI answers lean on the same things search does: an accurate website, a complete Google profile and a steady flow of reviews. Fund those first, then check how AI tools describe you.

Is social media still worth budgeting for?

Yes, as part of how customers check you out. In BrightLocal's 2026 survey, 24% of consumers said they visit a business's social media after reading positive reviews. Our advice is to budget for consistency over volume.

What should we measure if website clicks keep falling?

Count the actions that lead to revenue: calls, direction requests, bookings, form leads and walk in visits, plus review count and recency. Also check how AI tools describe you, because a correct description matters even when it sends no click.

When should a 2027 budget be set?

Now is a good time. Set the foundation items in December, review the first quarter's results in April, and adjust from there instead of locking every dollar in for twelve months.
takeaways: Gartner found budgets at 7.8% of revenue in 2026, but its sample is mostly companies above $1 billion in revenue, so it is not a rule for local businesses.
Forrester reports 91% of marketers expect budget increases in 2027 and recommends investing in visibility in AI answers.
BrightLocal found AI use for local recommendations rose from 6% to 45% in a year, while 97% of consumers still read reviews.
In our view, fund the foundation and Google profile first, then AI visibility, social and paid, and measure calls and bookings, not clicks alone.
